keyframe-node

attach this to a node inverted (so the nodes data ouput goes to this input, and this keyframe output goes to the nodes data inputs), the node should be designed to support full data chunk input and output

- inputs: {dataset:json, frameIndex:number}
- outputs: {dataset:json}
- data: {[frameIndex]: json}

- component:
- saveKeyframe: save the input data for the current frame
- deleteKeyframe: remove the data for the current frame
- play: when the frameIndex changes (and immediately), send the data for the current frame (interpolated), also ignore data coming in (as it should be a duplicate of what was sent)
- pause: stop sending data when frameIndex changes

prompt:

I have two images (with depth displacement) in a three.js scene from 2 frames of a real video. I am wanting to calculate the relative camera orientation so that all pixels projected from each camera line up.
The system is working manually and I can slowly adjust the 6 values (x,y,z pos, x,y,z rotation) to manually line up the image.
I want to automate this process, i.e. jitter those values while measuring pixel agreement (and move each value towards best agreement).
At first I just want to do this wholistically for the whole image, but eventually, I will do it patch wise and even segment the different objects in the scene that are moving independently.
For now, I am just trying to solve for the relative camera position and orentiation.
So, the only piece I need is to be able to get a score. I can do all the logic to jitter the position and have the 2 meshes in the scene for a candidate. But I need a way tow render and compare the pixel matches. (i.e. render B to A's camera and compare every pixel to the original image A => give me a match score for the overall image. (the score could be 0 is better, so basically, i just need a diff of all the pixels and then I could average their values to get an overall difference score).
Obviously I want to do this all on the gpu, this is easy on the cpu. I want to know how to do this with webgl2 (not webgpu).
Let's discuss the fastest way to do this at a very high framerate (the more matchScores I can calculate a second, the faster I can converge)

---

ok, this requires a gpu-cpu roundtrip to score it once. Is there a way I could send a batch of position, rotation adjustments (or maybe just tell it to randomly modify the 4x4 projection matrix) and it give me like 1000 attempts (the scores and their matrix inputs)
I mention the matrix, but I prefer the 6 x,y,z,rotX,rotY,rotZ better for human understanding (but if I could reconstruct those form a normalized matrix that would be fine too)
To be clear, mesh A is the origin (0 position and 0 rotation), so I only care about the relative position+rotation for mesh B (relative to A). So we could ignore the current mesh B position and rotation that is set by three js for this process.
Also if it is easier, we could go with just the raw rgb+depth textures and webgl2 shaders without threejs, I just want whatever is fastest to solve for it.

---

hmm, interesting. So I am interested in large pixel precise comparisons (so up to 4k image size with pixel percision).However, it would be helpful to work at a reduced resolution to get close to an approximate position before refining it futher.

However, you made me realize that I can always provide my own patches of large images.

So in addition to the 3pos3rot vector to try, I would also like to provide the image [x,y,w,h] bounds of the image area to test. This would allow me to easily sample at different scales or try different patch areas or focus on specific overlap areas, etc.

So a 64x64 comparison area is great as long as I can also specify the image bounds to compare.

solving for original camera fov and image crop

the iterative process of solving the relative position and orientation of 2 frames, depends on the camera fov and image crop

if those are changed, this will effect the alignment parameters

so in order to solve for the source camera, it is also needed to compare the flat image to the displaced image

ok, let's reset and talk about a single image first and figure out how to take the grayscale depth estimate and convert it into an actual how far the source object was from the pixel sensor.

for example, when I look at a photo, a standard depth estimate will show a gradient where the person projects out from a gradient of the background. But in 3d the person is 1.5m tall but the background is only 3m away from the screen. In reality, the background could be thousands of meters away.

At best the grayscale depth is only useful as a relative depth of the neighbor pixels and displaying it with a simple displacement map is heavily distorted.

So let's take what is known for sure. Each pixel in an image is a ray that goes directly from the camera sensor pixel location to the source of light in reality. So each pixel represents a ray projecting out for any distance.

The depth estimate is useful to give us local comparison, but a dark depth pixel could be anything from 50m to 5000m away (or more).

Of course the father the source of light is, the less the exact position of the camera matters, so we might just max out all background source rays at something like 100m (where the depth perspective is neglible)

it seems like it should be these steps:

- segment (edge detect) find all pixels where this is a jump in depth
- close curves (at ground or image border) 
- compress the cutout area scale to a local scale (and maybe linear instead of power)

hmm, but I don't want to do act like I can solve this at once, I want to be able to smooth the depth and correct it iteratively in the gpu.

- convert the depth to absolute distance to camera sensor units (in float32 meters) (assume single point camera sensor array).
- use a simpler consistent shader that projects the pixel position based only on this ray distance and the camera info (camera pos origin and orientation, fov of u/v, and uv of camera center)
